title: Span, Linear Independence, and Bases
---

Span, linear independence and bases are the building blocks of linear algebra. They describe vector spaces in terms of generating sets and coordinates. We define them both for finite lists of vectors $(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$, where order matters and repetitions are allowed (this is what coordinates and matrices need), and for arbitrary, possibly infinite, subsets $S \subseteq V$.

## <span class="num">4.6.1</span> Linear Combinations and Span

:::definition{4.6.1} Linear combination
A ***linear combination*** of vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_n \in V$ is a vector of the form $$a_1 v_1 + a_2 v_2 + \cdots + a_n v_n$$ with scalars $a_1, \ldots, a_n \in k$. For $n = 0$ the empty sum is $0$.
:::

:::definition{4.6.2} Span
The ***span*** of a subset $S \subseteq V$ is the set of all linear combinations of finitely many elements of $S$: $$\Span(S) = \left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i v_i : n \geq 0, \, a_i \in k, \, v_i \in S\right\}.$$ For a list $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ we write $\Span(v_1, \ldots, v_n) = \Span(\{v_1, \ldots, v_n\}) = \{a_1 v_1 + \cdots + a_n v_n : a_i \in k\}$. We say $S$ (or the list) ***spans*** $V$, or is a ***spanning set*** for $V$, if its span is $V$.
:::

Even when $S$ is infinite, only *finite* linear combinations are allowed; infinite sums have no meaning in a general vector space. Since the empty sum is $0$, we have $0 \in \Span(S)$ always, and $\Span(\emptyset) = \{0\}$.

:::proposition{4.6.3} The span is the smallest subspace containing $S$
For any subset $S \subseteq V$, $\Span(S)$ is a subspace of $V$ that contains $S$, and it is contained in every subspace of $V$ that contains $S$.
:::

:::proof
We have $0 \in \Span(S)$. A sum of two finite linear combinations of elements of $S$ is again one, and so is a scalar multiple of one: $c\sum a_i v_i + c'\sum a_i' v_i'$ is a linear combination of the finitely many vectors $v_i, v_i'$. So $\Span(S)$ is a subspace. Each $v \in S$ equals $1 \cdot v \in \Span(S)$. Finally, a subspace $W \supseteq S$ is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, hence (by induction on $n$) contains every linear combination $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i v_i$ with $v_i \in S$.
:::

Equivalently, $\Span(S)$ is the intersection of all subspaces containing $S$, which is a subspace by Proposition [4.5.11](/notes/math-55a/4-5-vector-spaces#proposition-4-5-11).

## <span class="num">4.6.2</span> Linear Independence

:::definition{4.6.4} Linear independence
A list of vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_n \in V$ is ***linearly independent*** if the only way to write $0$ as a linear combination of them is the trivial way: $$a_1 v_1 + a_2 v_2 + \cdots + a_n v_n = 0 \implies a_1 = a_2 = \cdots = a_n = 0.$$ A subset $S \subseteq V$ is ***linearly independent*** if every list of finitely many *distinct* elements of $S$ is linearly independent: for all $n \geq 1$, all distinct $v_1, \ldots, v_n \in S$ and all $a_1, \ldots, a_n \in k$, $$a_1 v_1 + \cdots + a_n v_n = 0 \implies a_1 = \cdots = a_n = 0.$$ A list or subset that is not linearly independent is ***linearly dependent***: some nontrivial finite linear combination of its elements is $0$.
:::

:::note
The word “distinct” matters. Without it, the relation $1 \cdot v + (-1) \cdot v = 0$ would make every nonempty set dependent. A list with a repeated vector, such as $(v, v)$, is linearly dependent, while the set $\{v, v\} = \{v\}$ is linearly independent whenever $v \neq 0$. For a list $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ of distinct vectors, the list is independent exactly when the set $\{v_1, \ldots, v_n\}$ is. The empty list and the empty set are linearly independent.
:::

:::note
Linear dependence means that some vector is a linear combination of the others. If $a_1 v_1 + \cdots + a_n v_n = 0$ with, say, $a_1 \neq 0$, then $$v_1 = -\frac{a_2}{a_1} v_2 - \cdots - \frac{a_n}{a_1} v_n,$$ so $v_1$ is redundant: it already lies in the span of the others.
:::

:::proposition{4.6.5} Characterizations of linear independence
The following are equivalent for vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_n \in V$:

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ are linearly independent;
2. no $v_j$ is a linear combination of the others;
3. the linear map $\Phi : k^n \to V$, $\Phi(a_1, \ldots, a_n) = \sum a_i v_i$, is injective.
:::

:::proof
(a) $\Rightarrow$ (c): If $\Phi(a) = \Phi(b)$, then $\sum (a_i - b_i) v_i = 0$, so $a_i = b_i$ for all $i$ by independence.

(c) $\Rightarrow$ (a): If $\sum a_i v_i = 0$, then $\Phi(a_1, \ldots, a_n) = 0 = \Phi(0, \ldots, 0)$, so all $a_i = 0$ by injectivity.

(a) $\Rightarrow$ (b): Suppose $v_j = \sum_{i \neq j} b_i v_i$. Then $\sum_{i \neq j} b_i v_i + (-1) v_j = 0$ is a nontrivial relation, since the coefficient of $v_j$ is $-1 \neq 0$, contradicting independence.

(b) $\Rightarrow$ (a): Suppose $\sum a_i v_i = 0$ with some $a_j \neq 0$. Then $v_j = -a_j^{-1} \sum_{i \neq j} a_i v_i$, contradicting (b).
:::

:::lemma{4.6.6} Adjoining a vector outside the span
If $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ are linearly independent and $v \notin \Span(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$, then $v_1, \ldots, v_n, v$ are linearly independent.
:::

:::proof
Suppose $a_1 v_1 + \cdots + a_n v_n + a v = 0$. If $a \neq 0$, then $v = -a^{-1}(a_1 v_1 + \cdots + a_n v_n) \in \Span(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$, a contradiction. So $a = 0$, and then $a_1 = \cdots = a_n = 0$ by independence of the $v_i$.
:::

:::proposition{4.6.7} Characterization of spanning
The following are equivalent for vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_n \in V$:

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ span $V$;
2. every $v \in V$ can be written as $\sum a_i v_i$ for some $a_i \in k$;
3. the linear map $\Phi : k^n \to V$, $\Phi(a_1, \ldots, a_n) = \sum a_i v_i$, is surjective.
:::

:::proof
Statement (b) is the definition of (a), and (c) says that every $v \in V$ is of the form $\Phi(a_1, \ldots, a_n) = \sum a_i v_i$, which is (b).
:::

## <span class="num">4.6.3</span> Bases

:::definition{4.6.8} Basis
A ***basis*** of $V$ is a linearly independent subset $\mathcal{B} \subseteq V$ that spans $V$. Similarly, a list $(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ is a basis of $V$ if it is linearly independent and spans $V$; equivalently, the linear map $\Phi : k^n \to V$, $(a_1, \ldots, a_n) \mapsto \sum a_i v_i$, is bijective.
:::

When we speak of a finite basis we usually mean a list, so that its elements come in a definite order.

:::proposition{4.6.9} Unique representation
A subset $\mathcal{B} \subseteq V$ is a basis if and only if every $v \in V$ can be written *uniquely* as a linear combination of distinct elements of $\mathcal{B}$; more precisely, there is a unique family of scalars $(a_b)_{b \in \mathcal{B}}$, only finitely many of them nonzero, with $v = \sum_{b \in \mathcal{B}} a_b b$. In particular, if $(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ is a basis of $V$, then every $v \in V$ can be written uniquely as $$v = a_1 v_1 + a_2 v_2 + \cdots + a_n v_n$$ with $a_i \in k$. The scalars $(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ are the ***coordinates*** of $v$ with respect to this basis.
:::

:::proof
Suppose $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis. Existence of an expression is the spanning property. If $v = \sum_b a_b b = \sum_b a_b' b$, then $\sum_b (a_b - a_b') b = 0$, a finite linear combination of distinct elements of $\mathcal{B}$; by independence, $a_b = a_b'$ for all $b$.

Conversely, suppose every vector has a unique expression. Then $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V$. If $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i = 0$ with distinct $b_i \in \mathcal{B}$, this is an expression of $0$; comparing it with the expression in which all coefficients are $0$, uniqueness gives $a_i = 0$ for all $i$. So $\mathcal{B}$ is independent. The statement for a list $(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ is proved in the same way.
:::

:::note
For an arbitrary subset $S \subseteq V$, let $k^{(S)}$ be the space of functions $a : S \to k$ with $a(s) \neq 0$ for only finitely many $s$. The map $k^{(S)} \to V$, $a \mapsto \sum_{s \in S} a(s)\, s$, is linear; $S$ spans $V$ if and only if it is surjective, $S$ is linearly independent if and only if it is injective, and $S$ is a basis if and only if it is bijective. For $S = \{v_1, \ldots, v_n\}$ with distinct $v_i$, this is the map $\Phi : k^n \to V$ above.
:::

:::example{4.6.10}
**Standard basis of $k^n$:** The vectors $$e_1 = (1, 0, \ldots, 0), \quad e_2 = (0, 1, 0, \ldots, 0), \quad \ldots, \quad e_n = (0, \ldots, 0, 1)$$ form the ***standard basis*** of $k^n$: every vector $(a_1, \ldots, a_n) = a_1 e_1 + \cdots + a_n e_n$, and this is the only way to write it as a linear combination of the $e_i$.
:::

:::example{4.6.11}
**A non-standard basis of $k^2$:** If $\mathrm{char}(k) \neq 2$, the vectors $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$ also form a basis of $k^2$: every vector can be written as $$(a, b) = \tfrac{a + b}{2}(1, 1) + \tfrac{a - b}{2}(1, -1),$$ and if $c(1, 1) + d(1, -1) = 0$, then $c + d = 0 = c - d$, so $2c = 0$ and $c = d = 0$. In characteristic $2$ this fails: there $-1 = 1$, so $(1, -1) = (1, 1)$ and the list is linearly dependent.
:::

:::example{4.6.12}
**Bases of polynomial spaces:** The polynomials $1, x, x^2, \ldots, x^n$ form a basis of $k[x]_{\leq n}$, and the infinite set $\{1, x, x^2, x^3, \ldots\}$ is a basis of $k[x]$. Indeed, every polynomial is a *finite* linear combination of monomials, and a linear combination $\sum_{i} a_i x^{n_i}$ of distinct monomials is the polynomial whose coefficients are the $a_i$, which is $0$ only if every $a_i = 0$.
:::

:::example{4.6.13}
In $k^\infty$, let $e_n$ be the sequence with $1$ in position $n$ and $0$ elsewhere. The set $\{e_0, e_1, e_2, \ldots\}$ is linearly independent, but it spans only the eventually zero sequences: a finite linear combination of the $e_n$ has only finitely many nonzero terms. So it is a basis of the subspace of eventually zero sequences, and not of $k^\infty$.
:::
